item.title: Sidewall Metrology Protocol for Superconducting Qubit Devices
item.description: arXiv:2610.26223v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sidewall morphology is a potentially important factor influencing superconducting qubit performance, yet its quantitative characterization remains challenging due to the absence of standardized measurement protocols. In this work, we develop a scanning probe microscopy-based measurement framework for the quantitative characterization of superconducting qubit sidewalls. The framework introduces a refined root mean square lateral sidewall roughness descriptor and a new curvature-equivalent radius for quantifying vertical sidewall morphology. The descriptors and measurement procedures are applied to different components of qubit devices, forming the basis of a proposed sidewall characterization protocol. This provides a foundation for quantitative comparisons of fabrication processes across laboratories, enabling future investigations of correlations between sidewall geometry and qubit performance.

item.title: Spatiotemporal Imaging of Thermally Driven Metal-Insulator Phase Domain Propagation in VO2
item.description: arXiv:2610.26367v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Achieving a detailed picture of the nature and dynamics of phase boundaries remains a major challenge, particularly solid-solid transitions central to phase-change materials. Here, we use stroboscopic optical scattering microscopy and finite-element simulations to study the nonlinear thermally driven motion of the mesoscale insulator-metal phase boundary in VO2 thin films. We visualize the lateral spatiotemporal evolution of a diffraction-limited photoinduced metallic phase domain, resolving its outward propagation, contraction, and ultimate disappearance. The phase boundary dynamics are governed by heat flow, which can be controlled by excitation fluence, film thickness, and substrate thermal conductivity. Parameter-free agreement between the data and nonlinear thermal transport simulations identify the phase boundary transport as locally diffusive under this regime. We quantify how the latent heat acts as a thermal inertia, suppressing transport and prolonging the phase coexistence. Paradoxically, despite being driven by the underlying thermal gradient locally described by Fourier's law, the mesoscale phase front propagates faster than expected from thermal diffusion. This phenomenon arises from the distinction between temperature-field evolution and phase-boundary isotherm motion. These results establish a link between heat dissipation and mesoscale phase-front motion, providing a framework for controlling phase-transition kinetics relevant to photonics applications of VO2. We anticipate that this approach generalizes to a broad class of first- and second-order transitions.

item.title: Coupling Evaporation, Chemical Reactions, and Crystallization: A Population-Balance Framework Applied to Two-Step Perovskite Crystallization
item.description: arXiv:2610.26591v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A limited understanding of how evaporation couples to crystallization pathways hampers control over the formation of solution-processed perovskite photoactive layers. Identifying these mechanisms-and learning how to select and tune them-is essential for achieving the desired crystal morphology and, ultimately, improving solar-cell performance and stability. To investigate crystallization pathways in evaporating thin films, we develop a simple and general zero-dimensional population-balance model that couples evaporation, chemical reactions, and crystallization. We use the model to explore a range of parameters for a solvent-solute system that follows a two-step crystallization pathway: solvent evaporation first induces formation of a crystalline precursor, which subsequently recrystallizes into the final phase. The model predicts the evolution of the film composition during drying and provides quantitative LaMer curves. Based on these results, we introduce a vocabulary of "supply limitations" and "rate limitations" that enables the interpretation of crystallization kinetics in terms of the governing process conditions.
item.dc:creator: K. Segadlo, O. J. J. Ronsin, J. Harting

item.title: Strain-induced disorder from Schottky gates on high mobility 2DEGs
item.description: arXiv:2610.26607v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electrostatic gates on two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) in GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures are essential for numerous studies of correlation driven phenomena, many performed within the fractional quantum Hall effect. However, the most commonly used type of gates, the metallic Schottky gate, has the propensity to adversely impact the electron mobility and suppress the fractional quantum Hall states. Here we demonstrate through commensurability oscillations under specially designed nanostructured superlattice gates, that strain effects are responsible for the mobility reduction. The experimental results agree well with COMSOL Multiphysics simulations. In a regular, unpatterned gate the disordered, granular nature of the metal film fills the same role as the superlattice in creating a strain field penetrating down to the 2DEG, as we show with a simplified model. These results will help in understanding, improving and finding novel methods to reduce strain-induced disorder in gated high-mobility 2DEGs.

item.title: Challenging Atomistic Foundation Models on Disordered Carbons
item.description: arXiv:2610.26701v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise broad transferability, yet their out-of-domain reliability is hard to establish. Here, we use pure and O/H-containing disordered carbon spanning multiple phases, competing hybridisations and porous frameworks to stress-test six popular foundation MLIPs. We first screen all six on density functional theory (DFT) energy and force errors and binding curves, then subject four to melt-quench-anneal molecular dynamics and evaluate the resulting structural observables. Binding curves and O/H-containing trajectories reveal unphysical extrapolation and dynamical failures that low DFT energy and force errors fail to reveal. Of the models tested, MACE-MH-1 is the most consistently robust, with low DFT errors and stable MD. Despite differing architectures, OMAT-based models share structural biases, highlighting the importance of training coverage. All four models generate structures of nanoporous carbon that reproduce the principal experimental and specialised carbon potential signatures. Incorporating O/H leaves short-range order largely unchanged but shifts pore-size distributions towards larger pores. These results emphasise the need for application-specific validation and extend molecular dynamics modelling of nanoporous carbon towards experimentally realistic structures.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Hart, Samuel G. H. Brookes, Fabian L. Thiemann, Christoph Schran

item.title: A boundary integral method for computing electron repulsion integrals in heterogeneous dielectric environments
item.description: arXiv:2610.26745v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a boundary integral method for evaluating electron repulsion integrals (ERIs) in dielectric environments of piecewise constant permittivity. This generalizes conventional bare-Coulomb ERIs by incorporating screening from structured dielectric surroundings, such as the substrates and/or encapsulating layers present in modern two-dimensional-material devices. We formulate the problem as a second-kind boundary integral equation for the induced surface charge on the dielectric interfaces, and discretize it with a Nystr\"om method on adaptively refined panels. The incident potential generated by each smooth orbital source density is evaluated by a Fourier truncated-kernel method in or near to its source box, and by fast multipole method (FMM) accelerated quadrature farther away. The linear system is solved by a Krylov iteration also accelerated by the FMM. We focus on cuboidal device geometries, and retain efficiency at high aspect ratios via close-to-touching panel quadratures. We further develop a distributed pipeline that computes the full ERI tensor, comprising thousands of orbital pairs, embedded in a single dielectric geometry. We demonstrate the method on an effective three-layer graphene slab over a Si/SiO$_2$ heterojunction, focusing on the central graphene layer represented by $198$ $p_z$-like orbitals, retaining the $2613^2$ non-negligible entries of the $198^4$-sized ERI tensor. The model is resolved on $1.3$ million surface unknowns, achieving a relative error of $0.004\%$, at a cost of $22$ node-hours.
item.dc:creator: Xuanzhao Gao, Malte R\"osner, Jason Kaye, Alex Barnett

item.title: Physics-Constrained Modeling and Inference of the Equation of State for Dissociative Materials
item.description: arXiv:2610.26791v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Equations of state (EOSs) describe how a material's internal energy and pressure change with temperature and density. They are inputs to hydrodynamic simulations in materials science and planetary science. We model the ion-thermal free-energy term for dissociative materials, where molecular bonds break apart to form new species under extreme conditions. This term is governed by two latent physical processes, a molar-mass surface and a Debye-temperature curve, neither of which is observed directly. Instead, both must be recovered from internal energy and pressure, which are derivatives of the free energy, subject to thermodynamic constraints. Existing EOS tables are typically built through material-specific hand-tuning, a process that is tedious, does not scale across materials or conditions, and offers no guarantee of thermodynamic consistency. We propose a partitioned statistical framework that infers molar mass and Debye temperature directly from EOS data, guaranteeing thermodynamic consistency by construction. Local molar-mass behavior is captured with polynomial basis functions across domain partitions, while the Debye temperature is modeled with an I-spline basis. In simulations and a carbon dioxide case study, the method accurately recovers the underlying physical quantities, improves prediction of held-out energy and pressure data, and provides uncertainty quantification while scaling with EOS table size.
item.dc:creator: Jolypich Pek, Ben Seiyon Lee, Jason Bernstein, Philip Myint

item.title: Resolving the energy alignment between methylammonium lead iodide and C60: an in-situ photoelectron spectroscopy study
item.description: arXiv:2601.07755v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding and controlling the energy level alignment at interfaces between lead halide perovskites and electron transport layers is crucial for optimizing perovskite-based devices such as solar cells. In this work, we investigated the energy level alignment of C60 on in-situ cleaved MAPbI3 single crystals in multiple repeat experiments using photoelectron spectroscopy aiming to resolve inconsistencies reported in earlier studies. Our results show that both materials remain chemically stable upon interface formation, in contrast to the strong reactions typically seen when metals are evaporated on perovskite surfaces. By analyzing the Pb 4f and C 1s binding energies in detail, we determined that C60 consistently exhibits a downward energy shift toward MAPbI3, which works against efficient charge extraction. The magnitude of this shift, however, varies between different sample positions, highlighting that small variations in sample surfaces can lead to significant differences in energetic alignment. These findings underscore the decisive role of surface chemistry on interfacial energetics, explain performance variability in perovskite devices, and demonstrate the need to control and accurately measure surface properties. Furthermore, the observed energetic alignment can explain why further interface modification by charge blocking layers or surface passivation is needed for optimized device efficiencies.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Garc\'ia-Fern\'andez, Karen Radetzky, Stefania Riva, Birgit Kammlander, Brian Rydgren, Evelyn Johannesson, Rahul Mahavir Varma, H{\aa}kan Rensmo, Ute B. Cappel

item.title: Thermal Decoherence and Population Transfer of MeV Channeling Electrons in Diamond
item.description: arXiv:2602.16529v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Channeling radiation from MeV-regime electrons is governed by transitions between quantized transverse bound states, but experimental spectra are strongly modified by thermal diffuse scattering. To capture these open-system dynamics, a frozen-phonon multislice framework is combined with bound-state projection analysis to construct depth-dependent reduced density matrices in selected transverse manifolds. Beyond reproducing experimental channeling-radiation transition energies, this approach separates thermal population transfer, intra-manifold decoherence, and cross-manifold coherence loss. Applied to 16.9 MeV axial electron channeling in $\langle100\rangle$ diamond, the results show approximately exponential population decay from the initially occupied states, accompanied by strongly channel-dependent feeding among low-lying manifolds. Starting from a coherent superposition within the degenerate 2p manifold, stochastic symmetry breaking by thermal displacements drives the intra-manifold purity toward the maximally mixed limit, indicating rapid phase scrambling. Under 1s initialization, population transferred into the 2p and 3d manifolds remains internally close to maximally mixed, yet a weak residual 2p-3d cross-manifold coherence persists. This framework goes beyond static mean-field thermal broadening and provides a microscopic basis for evaluating population dynamics and coherence lifetimes in strongly quantized channeling-radiation systems.
item.dc:creator: Tadas Paulauskas

item.title: Data-Efficient Indentation Size Effect Mitigation in Steels Using Machine Learning and a Physics-Constrained Neural Network
item.description: arXiv:2604.27775v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Shallow nanoindentation, needed for thin layers, individual phases and small volumes, gives hardness inflated by the indentation size effect (ISE). The Nix-Gao correction reduces this inflation but requires deep indentations of the same material, often impossible in such samples. We present a data-efficient workflow, trained on a few reference materials, that predicts a high-load reference hardness from a single shallow indentation. Seven models were trained on 703 indentations (5-350 mN) on three steels (2.0-6.5 GPa): Ridge regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, two feed-forward networks, and two physics-constrained neural networks (PCNNs) that apply a bounded learned correction q as H_app/sqrt(1+q). Over five seeds, models were tested on an external steel not used for training and indented at different loads, in leave-one-steel-out folds, and on fused silica, an out-of-domain material where all models failed. Random Forest and XGBoost, the best on the development set, transferred worst over all loads (MAPE 10.2 and 8.5%), whereas Ridge regression, the PCNNs and one feed-forward network reached 3.7-4.8%; with three training steels, development-set accuracy thus did not indicate accuracy on an unseen steel. From only the external steel's 3-15 mN indentations, the smooth (non-tree) models estimated the reference within 0.03-0.19 GPa on average. The PCNNs matched the linear baseline within the training hardness range and were the most accurate for a held-out steel softer than the training steels, but failed for a harder one. The workflow uses no steel-specific inputs and can be retrained for other material classes.
item.dc:creator: Radmir Karamov, Tagir Karamov

item.title: Diversity-Aware Active Learning Builds Materials Datasets for Current and Future Objectives
item.description: arXiv:2605.05104v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Materials science data collection can be expensive, making dataset reuse and long-term utility important for future discovery. In practice, data collection often prioritizes properties of current interest while other properties are excluded from the acquisition process. This can produce datasets that are well suited for current objectives but lose information needed for properties of future interest. Here, we present how to construct datasets that remain informative for both. We develop and evaluate acquisition frameworks that combine predictive disagreement with diversity in material features, predicted outcomes, or both. We test these approaches across four DFT datasets and an experimental thermoelectric dataset. Diversity inclusion in dataset construction can reduce present and future objectives trade-off by preserving a broader range of materials and property behavior during acquisition. Across all datasets, the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II with disagreements and feature diversity (NSGA-II Dis. + diversity) framework developed in this work provides the most robust balance between current and future objectives. It maintains prediction performance above random sampling for current objectives while mitigating bias on excluded properties and, in many cases, improving their performance beyond random sampling. This diversity-aware acquisition framework provides a practical route to building materials datasets with unbiased quality entries and mitigating cold-start limitations in subsequent modeling and discovery campaigns.
item.dc:creator: Rafael Espinosa Casta\~neda, Ashley Dale, Hongchen Wang, Yonatan Kurniawan, Hao Wan, Runze Zhang, Adji Bousso Dieng, Kangming Li, Jason Hattrick-Simpers

item.title: Shape-Constrained Bayesian Active Learning of Self-Limiting Saturation Curves
item.description: arXiv:2606.26577v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Saturation curves, monotone responses that rise from zero to a plateau, recur across gas adsorption, enzyme kinetics, and self-limiting growth. Learning one from a few costly, noisy measurements is a common bottleneck. We present a Bayesian active-learning platform built on a penalized monotone I-spline. Non-negative weights make every posterior draw rise from zero and never fall, a survey measurement anchors the plateau in place of a flatness prior, and the input reaching any saturation level is read from the posterior by level crossing, assuming no kinetic form. Each measurement is placed where the surrogate is least certain, which beats random designs and edges a log-spaced grid of the same budget. One fixed configuration recovers five kinetically distinct regimes from twenty measurements to a saturation error of 0.037 to 0.041, below the output noise, and averages 0.045 on 250 curves from an unseen distribution. Running unconstrained Gaussian processes (GPs) and two unpenalized monotone bases through the same loop separates each ingredient's contribution. Logarithmic resolution and the roughness penalty carry the accuracy, while monotonicity guarantees a level crossing unique on every draw. The penalty keeps the surrogate the most accurate model at every noise level, and its second-order form centers the recommended input for saturation where a first-order penalty reads late (a bias of +0.32 s with 94% coverage, against +0.44 s and 64% for the matched unconstrained GP). Because the recommended input lies where the curve is nearly flat, no method can pin it down precisely, and we report it as a cost-indexed quantile with the probability of falling short.
item.dc:creator: Pouyan Navabi, Christos G. Takoudis

item.title: Bias Tunable Transport Modulation and Gas Selectivity in Layered BiOI: A DFT NEGF Study
item.description: arXiv:2608.03308v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding the interplay between adsorption energetics and charge-transport modulation is essential for the rational design of low-power and bias-tunable gas sensors. Here, we present a comprehensive first-principles study of gas selectivity in layered bismuth oxyiodide (BiOI) by integrating density functional theory with nonequilibrium Green's function transport calculations. The adsorption and bias-dependent transport responses toward NO2, NH3, CO2, and representative volatile organic compounds are systematically examined. While NH3 and NO2 exhibit strong chemisorption and localized electronic perturbations, CO2 interacts through weak physisorption, demonstrating that adsorption strength alone does not determine sensing performance. Instead, the evolution of transmission channels near the Fermi level governs the sensing response. Bias-dependent calculations reveal an electrically tunable sensitivity hierarchy, in which weakly adsorbed CO2 preserves conductive pathways and exhibits pronounced low-bias sensitivity despite minimal charge transfer. Recovery-time analysis further highlights the trade-off between transport modulation and reversibility for strongly adsorbed species. These results establish a transport-centered selectivity framework for layered BiOI and provide mechanistic insight into electric-field-controlled gas sensing under ambient conditions.
item.dc:creator: Jemal Yimer Damte, Ji\v{r}\'i Hou\v{s}ka, Pavel Baroch, Xue Yong

item.title: Theoretical study of nitrogen-vacancy spin coherence enhanced by vacancy aggregation in diamond using cluster-correlation expansion
item.description: arXiv:2609.24295v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Annealing a semiconductor makes its vacancies mobile; they aggregate into multi-vacancy complexes that often carry spin. Such centres are a magnetic-noise source for any spin qubit among them, in silicon and silicon carbide as well as in diamond, and they are accordingly blamed for NV- decoherence in irradiated and implanted diamond, with two coherence records credited to removing them. Cluster-correlation-expansion simulations driven by published electron-paramagnetic-resonance parameters invert that attribution. At a fixed paramagnetic spin density a multi-vacancy bath gives a Hahn-echo coherence time 3.1-7.1 times longer than a bath of isolated negative vacancies, over three decades of concentration. A bath dephases the qubit because its spins exchange spin projections with one another, and two can exchange only if their transition frequencies match. A fine-structure splitting shifts those frequencies. Were every defect on the same crystallographic site, all would shift alike and still match: worth only a factor 1.15. Real defects occupy symmetry-equivalent sites pointing in different directions, so neighbours land at different frequencies and stop exchanging: a further 2.7. What governs the coherence time is therefore the fraction of bath pairs sharing a transition frequency, not the zero-field splitting. Vacancy aggregation extends NV- spin coherence rather than shortening it.

item.title: Deep Generative Crystal Structure Prediction: A Benchmark Study and a Controlled Test of Prototype Dependence
item.description: arXiv:2609.26502v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep generative models are widely reported to enable de novo crystal structure prediction (CSP), but their capability has not been measured consistently against template-based methods. We evaluate 12 representative generative CSP models, spanning latent-variable, diffusion, flow-matching, autoregressive, and manifold random-walk architectures, against TCSP 2.0 on 180 test structures and a leakage-controlled subset of 46. All methods use identical structure-matching, symmetry, and consensus criteria. Template retrieval is the strongest single method, reaching 68.3% top-1 success; symmetry-aware EquiCSP (66.4%) and Uni-3DAR (62.9%) form the next tier. However, comparison with TCSP 2.0 shows that most structures correctly predicted by generative models are also correctly predicted by template substitution. Thus, the set of structures uniquely reachable by generation is small, limiting its practical advantage for discovering structures outside existing prototype libraries. To test the source of this performance, we removed entire stoichiometric prototype families from the training set and retrained the strongest generative model. Accuracy declined by 50-78% across four families, establishing that performance is substantially prototype-dependent. A small minority of structures survived removal of their prototype family, demonstrating a real but limited retrieval-independent predictive capacity. Present generative CSP models therefore function largely as implicit, softer-edged prototype libraries rather than genuinely de novo predictors. Enlarging this residual capacity, rather than aggregate match rate alone, is the central open problem.

item.title: Extraction of different electronic contributions to transport properties of transition metals from first principles
item.description: arXiv:2610.08249v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate transport properties calculations in transition metals require treating inter-orbital hybridization, which is often poorly captured by simplified single-band models. We propose an \textit{ab initio} approach combining maximally localized Wannier functions and the Allen's method to correctly account for this mixing, overcoming the artifacts inherent to the Souza-Marzari-Vanderbilt scheme. Our method enables efficient orbital-resolved analysis of transport spectral functions. Applied to face-centered cubic Pd and body-centered cubic Mo, we reveal universal scattering mechanisms despite distinct electronic structures in these metals. Crucially, the parallel addition of distinct scattering channels perfectly reproduces full Allen's method calculations, rigorously validating this decomposition. We show that the absence of a $d$-peak at Fermi level in Mo enhances $s$-$s$ scattering, while the same contribution to resistivity and electron thermal conductivity of Pd is close to the experimental data for Ag. Ultimately, the proposed method provides a universal and efficient tool for the microscopic analysis of electron-phonon scattering mechanisms in systems with strong hybridization between localized and delocalized electron states.
item.dc:creator: I. S. Galtsov, D. V. Minakov, P. R. Levashov

item.title: Temperature dependence of spin-model parameters in ferrimagnets
item.description: arXiv:2610.08582v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We compute the temperature dependence of effective spin-model parameters in two-sublattice ferrimagnets with antiparallel and inequivalent sublattice magnetizations using Green's-function theory. The effective intra- and intersublattice exchange interactions, together with the sublattice anisotropies, exhibit distinct thermal renormalizations arising from the different magnetic interactions and correlations of the two sublattices. Although these effective interaction parameters decrease monotonically with increasing temperature, their unequal renormalization produces a strongly nonmonotonic and polarization-dependent long-wavelength spin-wave response. In particular, the spin-wave exchange stiffness exhibits a strongly branch-dependent and nonmonotonic temperature dependence. One polarization develops an enhanced spin-wave stiffness in the vicinity of the angular momentum compensation region despite the monotonic thermal reduction of the underlying exchange interactions. The Green's-function predictions are in quantitative agreement with atomistic spin-dynamics simulations, which provide a numerical benchmark including thermally induced spin correlations within the underlying atomistic spin model. These results establish a direct connection between temperature-dependent atomistic interactions, long-wavelength spin-wave stiffness, and the effective parameters required for finite-temperature micromagnetic and multiscale modeling of ferrimagnetic materials.

item.title: Magnetic order in epitaxial (La2/3Sr1/3MnO3)3/(BaTiO3)3 trilayer heterostructures
item.description: arXiv:2610.23556v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The realization of artificial magnetic structures with high epitaxial quality and elevated critical temperatures remains a key challenge for spintronics. Here, we report the fabrication and characterization of epitaxial (La2/3Sr1/3MnO3)3/(BaTiO3)3 trilayer heterostructures grown by layer-by-layer laser ablation. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy, magnetization measurements, and neutron diffraction confirm their exceptional crystalline order and the absence of structural defects. Neutron diffraction reveals no antiferromagnetic at non-zero wavevector Bragg peaks, ruling out most antiferromagnetic configurations with a non zero wave vector Q. Magnetic hysteresis loops instead evidence a ferromagnetic order with a remanent moment of about 0.5 Bohr magneton per Mn atom at room temperature, persisting either in-plane or out-of-plane depending on the applied field. Our findings highlight neutron diffraction as a powerful tool for elucidating the magnetic structure of complex thin films and suggest that weak interlayer coupling through BaTiO3 leads to ferromagnetism with a high critical temperature (about 600 K).

item.title: Surface-extended Andreev bound states emerging from intrinsic surface superconductivity of PtBi$_2$
item.description: arXiv:2507.13843v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Intrinsic topological superconductivity remains one of the central open questions in condensed-matter physics. The three-dimensional Weyl semimetal PtBi$_2$ has recently been shown by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to host a superconducting gap that opens exclusively on its Fermi-arc surface states and exhibits a nodal structure, making it a promising platform for exploring unconventional and potentially topological superconductivity. However, despite these momentum-resolved insights, the real-space spectroscopic signatures of unconventional superconductivity in PtBi$_2$ remain unclear. Here, using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, we reveal a sizable and spatially homogeneous gap ($\Delta > 10\,\mathrm{meV}$) on atomically pristine terraces of PtBi$_2$. Within this gap, we detect surface-extended in-gap states exhibiting pronounced atomic-scale spatial modulation. Analysis of the tunneling spectra indicates that these states are most consistently interpreted as Andreev bound states within a superconducting gap. Further phenomenological modeling shows that their characteristic spectral features are naturally captured by a chiral pairing scenario. Our results establish a direct real-space connection between the superconducting gap and surface-extended quasiparticle states in PtBi$_2$, and provide new insight into the nature of its unconventional surface superconductivity. These findings highlight PtBi$_2$ as a versatile platform for exploring exotic quasiparticle excitations and potential Majorana physics.

item.title: Purely equatorial lasing in spherical liquid crystal polymer microlasers with bipolar refractive index profile
item.description: arXiv:2601.12673v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Liquid crystal whispering gallery mode (WGM) microlasers show high sensitivity to external stimuli and distinct spectral features, rendering them ideally suited for various sensing applications. They also offer intrinsic anisotropic optical properties, which can be used to shape and manipulate light even inside spatially highly symmetric structures. Here, we report the fabrication of a spherical bipolar liquid crystal polymer microlaser that tightly confines the optical path of WGMs to the equatorial plane. By controlled anchoring of the liquid crystal mesogens followed by polymerization, a fixed refractive index profile is formed within the spherical microcavity. Consequently, only transverse electric (TE) modes oscillating in the equatorial plane experience the high extraordinary refractive index, allowing to confine lasing into a single plane. Furthermore, we observe a characteristic splitting into sub-modes. By combining hyperspectral imaging, optical modeling, and theoretical calculations, we show that the observed sub-modes originate from the lifting of the energy degeneracy of azimuthal WGMs. The unique ability to confine lasing into a single plane makes these spherical microlasers independent of the exact position of the pump beam, which allows consistent localized sensing especially in combination with fast point scanning microscopes or inside highly dynamic biological environments.

item.title: AutoREC: A reinforcement learning platform for equivalent circuit model generation
item.description: arXiv:2604.27266v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper introduces AutoREC, an open-source Python platform for developing, training and evaluating reinforcement learning (RL) agents that automatically generate equivalent circuit models (ECMs) from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) data. Although ECMs are widely used to interpret EIS measurements, their identification typically relies on manual trial-and-error, requiring domain expertise and limiting scalability, particularly in autonomous experimental pipelines such as self-driving laboratories. In AutoREC, ECM generation is formulated as a Markov decision process in which an RL agent sequentially modifies a circuit topology based on the current state, available actions and feedback from the resulting model. The platform supports an end-to-end workflow encompassing EIS preprocessing with selectable impedance representations, agent setup and training, ECM generation for new measurements and visualization-based evaluation and analysis of agent decision-making. AutoREC implements a configurable Double Deep Q-Network agent with prioritized experience replay and a dedicated deadloop mitigation strategy for navigating the complex circuit-generation action space efficiently. To demonstrate the platform, we trained a representative agent on 1350 synthetic spectra from five reference circuit families, evaluated it on 150 held-out synthetic spectra and applied it to 32 previously unseen experimental spectra from battery, corrosion, oxygen evolution reaction and CO2 reduction systems. These case studies illustrate the end-to-end capabilities of AutoREC while revealing challenges associated with experimental complexity and limited training-data coverage. The demonstrated agent serves as a reference implementation; AutoREC provides an extensible foundation through which users can develop and evaluate agents tailored to their specific electrochemical systems and research objectives.

item.title: Solar photocatalytic disinfection of well water using immobilized TiO$_2$: A comparative field study with SODIS in Antananarivo
item.description: arXiv:2605.04089v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Access to safe drinking water remains a major challenge in rural areas of developing countries. This study investigates the feasibility of a simple, low-cost solar photocatalytic reactor coated with a commercial titanium dioxide (TiO$_2$) pigment for the disinfection of well water contaminated with fecal coliforms. A TiO$_2$ film was deposited on a glass plate using a straightforward acetone slurry method and exposed to natural sunlight in Antananarivo, Madagascar. The efficiency was compared with the conventional SODIS method (solar disinfection without catalyst). Water samples from ten different wells were characterized for physicochemical and bacteriological quality. After 10 minutes of solar exposure, the photocatalytic reactor reduced presumptive fecal coliform counts below the method detection limit ($<$1~CFU/100~mL) in all ten samples tested, whereas the SODIS control reduced the initial count by approximately 51\% in a representative sample. While disinfection kinetics varied slightly with water turbidity and pH, inactivation below the detection limit was consistently achieved. Pearson correlation analysis showed no statistically significant linear correlation between the inactivation rate constant and any measured water-quality parameter (all $p > 0.4$). The results demonstrate that even a non-uniform, low-purity TiO$_2$ coating significantly accelerates bacterial inactivation under solar radiation, offering a promising and affordable household-scale treatment technology for low-resource settings. However, longer-term validation, catalyst stability, dark-control assessment, and leaching studies are still required before widespread implementation can be recommended.

item.title: Only skin deep? Depth-resolved photo-oxidation of 3D printed polymers PLA, ABS, PETG, HIPS and PC after 322 days of continuous UV exposure
item.description: arXiv:2606.00068v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study investigates the effect of long-term UV radiation exposure on the mechanical and structural properties of selected polymeric materials - PLA, ABS, ABST, PETG, HIPS and PC - fabricated using 3D-print based Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) method. Existing research in the field of polymers weathering has predominantly examined combined degradation factors (UV irradiation, humidity and thermal cycling) over the timescales rarely exceeding a few months, which prevents attribution of property changes to individual agents. To isolate the contribution of UV radiation specifically, samples were exposed up to 7744 consecutive hours (i.e. 322 days) of UV irradiation in an environmental cell with controlled humidity and temperature. The mechanical properties were characterized using nanoindentation, which allows for spatially resolved measurements of hardness and elastic modulus in the near-surface region, thereby enabling the detection of degradation gradients on the order of tens of micrometers. The lack of methodological consistency in the current literature hinders the cross-material comparison; this study addresses the gap by applying nanoindentation uniformly across wide range of selected materials prepared and tested under identical conditions, while studying these properties after a very long exposure to UV radiation.

item.title: Microstructure-Conditioned Surrogate Models for Graded Multiscale Optimization of Mycelium Composites
item.description: arXiv:2607.13688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Emerging sustainable materials increasingly rely on engineered hierarchy and microstructure to achieve control of their properties and mechanical behavior. Optimizing these materials with controllable microstructures requires efficient multiscale simulations. Data-driven surrogate models for the microscale can accelerate multiscale simulations, but require large amounts of data even for a fixed microstructure. When a range of microstructures is considered, as is the case in multiscale optimization, even more data is needed to train a surrogate. To overcome this challenge, we condition a hybrid physics-data surrogate on microstructural variables using a hypernetwork. This approach enables accurate predictions of multiscale mechanical behavior for a mycelium-woodchip composite material, even when trained on small datasets. The conditioned surrogate makes multiscale simulations of functionally graded structures tractable, and we validate it against a full FE^2 simulation. We optimize a graded multiscale disk, and reduce the peak stress by 43% compared to one with a random microstructure. Then, we go one step further, conditioning the network directly on manufacturing variables that can have a complex influence on the microstructure. This is a practical route to engineer the microscale for desired macroscale behavior. This contribution highlights the benefits of microarchitectured structures and demonstrates how conditioned surrogate models enable their multiscale optimization, which will accelerate the development and design of future sustainable materials and structures.

item.title: Picosecond-resolved entanglement distribution over an urban free-space channel
item.description: arXiv:2607.21093v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time-evolving entangled states describe quantum particles whose correlations evolve in time according to a well-defined dynamics. Such states can be generated in a variety of physical systems and are promising resources for several quantum technologies, ranging from quantum clock synchronization to quantum communication. However, their full potential is currently limited by the fact that the entanglement dynamics often occur on timescales comparable to the achievable synchronization precision, especially in experiments aimed at distributing entanglement through noisy urban channels. In this context, accurate timing is not merely a technical detail, but a fundamental requirement for faithfully observing and exploiting the underlying quantum correlations. Here, we demonstrate the faithful distribution of a fast-evolving entangled state over a 270 m free-space channel connecting two buildings in the center of Rome. The developed system incorporates a synchronization device capable of achieving sub-50 ps timing accuracy between the two ends of the link while simultaneously supporting channel stabilization. Our results demonstrate that time-evolving entanglement can be reliably transmitted through a noisy urban free-space channel, representing an important benchmark toward long-distance free-space quantum communication and the future implementation of time-correlated entangled states in demanding scenarios such as satellite-based quantum networks.

item.title: Smoothed truncated Coulomb potential for periodic Gaussian-basis Hartree--Fock exchange
item.description: arXiv:2609.00203v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Truncated Coulomb (TC) potentials reduce finite-size errors and accelerate thermodynamic-limit convergence in periodic Hartree--Fock (HF) calculations, but their use with Gaussian basis sets is complicated by the evaluation of electron repulsion integrals (ERIs), particularly for nonspherical truncation domains and all-electron calculations. We introduce the smoothed truncated Coulomb (sTC) potential as a systematically improvable approximation to a parent TC potential. A real-space Gaussian convolution smooths the sharp truncation boundary, and a single dimensionless parameter, $\eta$, controls the width of the smoothing window, which can be tightened to systematically approach the TC reference. The smoothing by sTC enables a dual-space algorithm for evaluating periodic Gaussian-basis ERIs that requires neither a large plane-wave basis nor new molecular integral kernels and is applicable to both pseudopotential and all-electron calculations, including the important Wigner--Seitz-cell truncation boundaries. Benchmarks spanning insulating, semiconducting, layered, metallic, and molecular-crystal systems show that sTC-based HF closely reproduces TC results in pseudopotential calculations and extends TC-quality calculations to all-electron settings. Across these systems, sTC substantially improves thermodynamic-limit convergence relative to the probe-charge Ewald method while remaining practical for all-electron calculations in which direct TC-based calculations are computationally challenging.

item.title: Theory of exciton-exciton interactions with nontrivial electronic bands
item.description: arXiv:2610.13246v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Excitons are bound electron-hole pairs in semiconductors whose interactions influence optical properties and determine their collective behavior and emergent correlated phases. Despite the theoretical and experimental significance of these phenomena, a microscopic theory of exciton-exciton interactions that takes into account the full composite nature of these quasiparticles in systems with an arbitrary single-particle Hamiltonian is lacking. Here, we present a general theory of exciton-exciton interactions that builds upon our previous publication [Physical Review B 113, 155440 (2026)], which applied only to conventional semiconductors with weak band hybridization. By contrast, the theory presented here is valid in virtually any crystalline semiconducting system and can be applied to the study of biexciton formation and correlated excitonic phases in systems where band topology, quantum geometry, and moir\'e effects play a significant role. In addition to the analytical theory, we also present results in simple systems with flat bands with a nontrivial quantum metric and show that the biexcitonic spectrum differs strongly from that in the case without quantum geometry. Our theory paves the way for accurate quantitative calculations of biexciton spectra and excitonic many-body phases in modern condensed-matter systems.
item.dc:creator: L. Maisel Licer\'an, H. T. C. Stoof

item.title: Seismology of Glasses
item.description: arXiv:2610.19602v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Aging and relaxation of glasses proceed through localized rearrangements that also generate long-ranged mechanical responses in their surroundings. We develop a theory that treats these rearrangements as internal microseismic sources, and thereby separates the direct effects emerging from an event from the effects from the far-field displacements it generates. These far-field disturbances propagate and relax through the viscoelastic medium through which they move, producing a stochastic background of weak but numerous perturbations at any given location. Combining the description of local events from the Random First Order Transition theory with this propagating background, we derive a unified equation for the dynamical structure factor of a relaxing glass. The theory identifies a finite wave-vector and time window in which the growing viscoelastic far-field disturbances can produce compressed exponential relaxation, which has been observed using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy. At higher wave vectors that resolve local jumps, heterogeneity of the local event dynamics instead produces stretched exponential relaxation. The crossover between these behaviors depends on the event statistics and the scattering phase accumulated across the region reached through viscoelastic propagation from the numerous distant sources.

item.title: Magnetic field induced modulation of heat transport in CrPS$_4$ probed by TaIrTe$_4$ transverse Seebeck thermometry
item.description: arXiv:2610.19833v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding and controlling heat flow in low-dimensional magnetic materials is central to thermoelectrics and spin caloritronics. One of the challenges is the absence of sensitive probes of small, field-dependent modulations in thermal transport. Here we demonstrate transverse Seebeck thermometry using exfoliated TaIrTe$_4$ as a probe of thermal conductivity modulated by an external magnetic field on a van der Waals magnet, CrPS$_4$. With a temperature gradient oriented at $45^\circ$ to its principal crystallographic axes, TaIrTe$_4$ exhibits a transverse thermopower exceeding $200~\mathrm{\mu V\,K^{-1}}$ for 900 nm wide and 30 $\mu$m long electrodes, enabling precise detection of variations in the local temperature gradients. Exploiting this with CrPS$_4$ in a nonlocal geometry, we resolve distinct field dependent thermal conductivity changes associated with both the spin-flip and spin-flop magnetic transitions which we attribute to variations in the magnon$-$phonon coupling in CrPS$_4$. At 5 K, the transverse Seebeck response is modulated by more than 8$\%$ by an external magnetic field, demonstrating strong magnetic control of heat transport in CrPS$_4$. This all van der Waals platform offers high sensitivity to modulations of thermal conductivity and a broad adaptability to a wide range of exfoliated magnetic systems.
